name: Disposable gloves (nitrile, latex, vinyl)
summary: Thin single-use gloves of nitrile, latex or vinyl that keep body fluids, dirt and light chemical splashes off your skin for a short time.
uses: Blood and body fluids: a barrier for first aid and cleaning up. It won't stop a needle or a sharp edge (FDA GLOVES, ISHN NEEDLES)
Chemicals: splash protection only. Thin nitrile lets acetone, methanol, xylene and dichloromethane through in about a minute; change at once if splashed (KC NITRILE)
Fuel and oil: thin nitrile held diesel, kerosene and mineral spirits for over an hour in tests, so it suits short jobs, not soaking (KC NITRILE)
Bleach, caustic soda and 47% sulfuric acid (Ansell calls it battery acid): held for hours in tests. Concentrated sulfuric or 70% nitric acid: through in about a minute (KC NITRILE, ANSELL CRG)
Latex can cause allergy, rarely fatal. Vinyl leaks far more often than nitrile or latex once worked (OSHA LATEX SHIB, REGO 1999, KORNIEWICZ 1990)
Single use: don't wash or reuse them. Take any gloves off near spinning machines (OSHA BBP, OSHA 3170)
identify: Thin, stretchy gloves sold loose in boxes. Read the box, not the colour. Medical exam gloves name a standard: ASTM D6319 nitrile (ASTM D6319), D3578 latex rubber (ASTM D3578), D5250 vinyl or PVC (ASTM D5250), D6977 polychloroprene (ASTM D6977); D6978 is the chemotherapy-drug test (ASTM D6978). European medical gloves cite EN 455 (SATRA EN 455). In Canada all medical gloves are licensed Class II medical devices, and non-medical gloves fall outside the Medical Device Regulations (HC MEDICAL GLOVES). A chemical claim shows the EN ISO 374 flask with Type A, B or C and letters for the chemicals passed, such as K for 40% caustic soda; Type C needs only one chemical held for 10 minutes (EJENDALS EN 374). A biohazard symbol with VIRUS means it passed the virus test (EJENDALS EN 374). In Europe latex boxes must carry an allergy warning and may not claim to be low-allergy (SATRA EN 455). Gloves marked hypoallergenic, mostly old stock, may still be latex: it once meant fewer chemical additives, not latex-free (OSHA LATEX SHIB). The FDA banned powdered medical gloves in 2016 (FDA GLOVES). Thicker gloves protect more, thinner ones give more feel (HSE GLOVES). Note any expiry or manufacture date.
test: Check the date and where the box sat. Makers give latex about 3 years and nitrile or vinyl a nominal 5 years in cool, dark storage; heat over about 32 °C (90 °F), sunlight, ozone from motors and damp all shorten it (S+H SHELF LIFE). Test one or two from each box. A good glove looks normal, stretches without surface cracks and goes on without tearing. Aged ones tear easily, crack when stretched or, if powder-free, turn gooey (S+H SHELF LIFE). Leak check: trap air by swinging the glove by its cuff, then squeeze and listen and feel for leaks (CCOHS GLOVES), or fill it with water and watch for drips, as the EN 455 hole test does (SATRA EN 455). Fit: snug, not tight; oversized gloves fold and get in the way (HSE GLOVES). In use, change them as soon as they tear or get splashed with a chemical (FDA GLOVES, KC NITRILE). Never wash, disinfect, share or reuse them (FDA GLOVES, OSHA BBP). Wash your hands after taking them off (FDA GLOVES).

decay.note: Makers give latex about 3 years and nitrile or vinyl about 5 in cool, dark storage; heat, sunlight and ozone in unheated buildings and cars age them faster (S+H SHELF LIFE).

improvise: Better than nothing: thick reusable household rubber gloves for body fluids and cleaning. Natural latex resists most water solutions of acids, alkalis and salts (OSHA 3151), but is not recommended for concentrated sulfuric or 70% nitric acid and does poorly against solvents and fuels (OSHA 3151, ANSELL CRG). For any real chemical work, a chemical glove matched to the chemical is far better than any disposable. Plastic bags over your hands tear and have no tested resistance: use them only to keep dirt off, never as protection from solvents. Useless: cloth and leather gloves soak liquids up and hold them against your skin (HC PESTICIDE GLOVES). No glove makes a needle safe: fine needles go through thin nitrile, latex and vinyl (ISHN NEEDLES), so keep sharps out of your hands: use pliers or tongs, as OSHA directs for broken glass (OSHA BBP). If you are allergic to latex, don't use latex gloves, even old ones labelled hypoallergenic (OSHA LATEX SHIB); some people allergic to banana, avocado, kiwi or chestnut also react to latex (CCOHS LATEX). If you have no gloves at all, keep contact short, wash your hands with soap and water straight away, and keep cuts covered.
